mcqs.q: The periodontal ligament (PDL) is best described as connective tissue that:
opts: Surrounds the root and connects it to the alveolar bone
mcqs.explain: The PDL is a vascular, highly cellular connective tissue surrounding the root and connecting it to the inner wall of the alveolar bone — providing continuity between cementum and bone.

mcqs.q: The average width of the PDL is about:
opts: 0.2 mm (range 0.15–0.38 mm), thinnest in the middle of the root
mcqs.explain: The PDL is about 0.2 mm wide (range 0.15–0.38 mm) and is thinnest in the middle region of the root.

mcqs.q: The PDL space becomes WIDER in:
mcqs.explain: Hyperfunction widens the PDL space; reduced function or an unerupted tooth narrows it.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, the normal PDL appears as a:
opts: Thin radiolucent line around the root
mcqs.explain: The normal PDL appears as a thin radiolucent line; widening/thickening of this line suggests pathology.

mcqs.q: The principal fibres of the PDL are composed mainly of:
mcqs.explain: The principal fibres are mainly collagen type I, arranged in bundles with a wavy course in longitudinal section.

mcqs.q: The terminal portions of principal fibres embedded in cementum and bone are called:
mcqs.explain: The terminal portions of the principal fibres inserted into cementum and bone are termed Sharpey's fibres.

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of collagen assembly is:
mcqs.explain: Inside fibroblasts, tropocollagen aggregates into microfibrils, then fibrils, then fibres, which group into bundles — giving tensile strength greater than steel.

mcqs.q: Which is the LARGEST group of principal fibres, bearing the brunt of vertical masticatory stress?
mcqs.explain: Oblique fibres are the largest group; they run from cementum coronally to bone and convert vertical chewing stress into tension on the alveolar bone.

mcqs.q: Transseptal fibres are unique because they:
opts: Extend between adjacent teeth over the crest and are rebuilt even after bone loss
Run from cementum to bone at the apex
mcqs.explain: Transseptal fibres run interproximally over the alveolar crest into the cementum of adjacent teeth and are reconstructed even after periodontal bone destruction.

mcqs.q: The function of the alveolar crest fibres is to:
opts: Prevent extrusion and resist lateral tooth movement
mcqs.explain: Alveolar crest fibres extend obliquely from cementum (just below the junctional epithelium) to the crest, preventing extrusion and resisting lateral movement.

mcqs.q: Apical fibres of the PDL:
opts: Radiate from cementum to bone at the apex and are absent on incompletely formed roots
mcqs.explain: Apical fibres radiate irregularly from the cementum to the bone at the apex; they do not occur on incompletely formed roots.

mcqs.q: Interradicular fibres are found:
opts: In the furcation areas of multirooted teeth
At the apex of single-rooted teeth
mcqs.explain: Interradicular fibres fan out from the cementum to the bone in the furcation areas of multirooted teeth.

mcqs.q: Regarding elastin in the PDL:
opts: There is no mature elastin; only the immature forms oxytalan and elaunin occur
Mature elastin is the main fibre
mcqs.explain: The PDL contains no mature elastin; two immature forms — oxytalan and elaunin — are present.

mcqs.q: The MOST common cell in the periodontal ligament is the:
mcqs.explain: Fibroblasts are the most common PDL cells; they are oriented along the principal fibres and both synthesize and phagocytose collagen.

mcqs.q: A distinctive dual ability of PDL fibroblasts is that they:
opts: Synthesize collagen AND phagocytose/degrade old collagen
mcqs.explain: PDL fibroblasts synthesize new collagen and can phagocytose 'old' collagen fibres, degrading them by enzyme hydrolysis — allowing rapid turnover.

mcqs.q: The epithelial rests of Malassez are remnants of:
mcqs.explain: The epithelial rests of Malassez are remnants of Hertwig's root sheath; they diminish with age and can proliferate to form periapical/lateral root cysts.

mcqs.q: When stimulated, the epithelial rests of Malassez may participate in forming:
mcqs.explain: Although usually quiescent, epithelial rests can proliferate and participate in the formation of periapical and lateral root cysts.

mcqs.q: The ground substance of the PDL has a high water content of about:
mcqs.explain: The ground substance is ~70% water and consists of glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid, proteoglycans) and glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin).

mcqs.q: Calcified masses sometimes found in the PDL, adherent to or detached from the root, are:
mcqs.explain: Cementicles are calcified masses within the PDL ground substance, either attached to or free from the root surface.

mcqs.q: The PDL receives its blood supply from all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Branches directly from the lingual nerve
Apical vessels (that also supply the pulp)
mcqs.explain: PDL blood comes from three sources: apical vessels, intra-alveolar (perforating) vessels, and gingival vessels — not from a nerve.

mcqs.q: The sensory nerves of the PDL are responsible for:
mcqs.explain: PDL sensory fibres mediate touch, pressure, pain and proprioception; autonomic fibres supply the vessels.

mcqs.q: A feature that makes the PDL unique is that it:
opts: Contains cells that both form and resorb cementum and bone
mcqs.explain: The PDL is unique in housing cells that both form and resorb the two adjacent mineralized tissues (cementum and bone), with fibres in a specific orientation.

mcqs.q: Horizontal principal fibres run:
opts: At right angles to the long axis of the tooth, from cementum to bone
mcqs.explain: Horizontal fibres extend at right angles to the long axis of the tooth, from the cementum to the alveolar bone.

mcqs.q: The small collagen fibres running in all directions among the principal fibres form the:
mcqs.explain: Small collagen fibres associated with the principal fibres run in all directions and form the indifferent fibre plexus.

saqs.q: Define the PDL and give its width.
saqs.a: A complex, vascular, cellular connective tissue that surrounds the root and connects it to the alveolar bone (continuity between cementum and bone). Width ~0.2 mm (0.15–0.38 mm), thinnest mid-root.

saqs.q: List the six principal fibre groups of the PDL.
saqs.a: Transseptal, alveolar crest, horizontal, oblique, apical, and interradicular fibres.

saqs.q: Which fibre group is the largest and what is its function?
saqs.a: The oblique fibres — they bear the brunt of vertical masticatory stress, transforming it into tension on the alveolar bone.
The terminal portions of principal fibres embedded in cementum and bone.

saqs.q: Name the cell types of the PDL.
saqs.a: Synthetic (fibroblasts — most common, osteoblasts, cementoblasts), resorptive (osteoclasts, cementoclasts), defence (mast cells, macrophages), epithelial rests of Malassez, and progenitor (UMC) cells.

saqs.q: Describe the ground substance of the PDL.
saqs.a: A gel-like matrix (~70% water) of glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid, proteoglycans) and glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin); may contain cementicles.

saqs.q: Give the three sources of blood supply to the PDL.
saqs.a: Apical vessels (also supplying the pulp), intra-alveolar (perforating) vessels, and gingival vessels.
